newsitem.title: POLAND: Pope has moving reunion with with old schoolmates.
newsitem.headline: Pope has moving reunion with with old schoolmates.

text.p: Pope John Paul, on a sentimental journey home, had an emotional reunion on Friday with some of the surviving classmates who attended elementary school with him in pre-war Poland some 70 years ago.

The 13 old friends who also grew up in the Pope's hometown of Wadowice travelled to the Zakopane mountain resort in southern Poland to see the most famous son their school, their town and their country have produced.
"It was very moving," said chief Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls. "There were hugs all over the place".

Some of the old friends brought albums with photographs from their school days in the small nearby town of Wadowice, where the Pope was born Karol Wojtyla on May 18, 1920. The Pope later signed some of the albums.
One of the 13 included a woman who later also acted in a theatre group when the future Pope, who was fascinated by the stage and wrote for it, attended university in Krakow.
The meeting was an emotional high point for the 77-year-old Pope, who is on the seventh day of an 11-day trip home which has centred on some of the areas he held dear in his youth.

It took place at a church-owned retreat where the Pope, who seems to have been invigorated by the scent and feel of his homeland since his arrival, is wrapping up a two-day stop for mostly private time in the mountain area.
He also had a meeting with a monsignor who studied for the priesthood secretly along with the future Pontiff in Krakow during the Nazi occupation of their country in World War Two.

A small group of astonished tourists were delighted when the Pope took a cable car to Kasprowy, one of the peaks overlooking Zakopane, and paused at the top to drink tea and take in the panorama before visiting a convent down below.
Navarro-Valls, who accompanied the Pontiff, said that while riding up in the cable car John Paul told his aides: "I remember when sometimes I used to do this on foot."
"He is enjoying himself. He is having a good time," Navarro-Valls said.
Earlier on Friday the Pope presided at a big open-air mass and touched on an issue dividing Poles as they prepare for parliamentary elections in September: the influence of the Church.

In his sermon before some 200,000 people gathered around a hill used as a ski jump, he referred to a controversy that erupted after the 1989 fall of communism over the display of crucifixes in schools and public offices.

The first non-communist governments allowed a return of crucifixes in public buildings as a symbol of Poland's predominantly Catholic heritage and as a tribute to the role the Church had played in Marxism's downfall.
This decision was contested by the leftist opposition and some intellectuals who wanted a clearer separation of Church and state. But the crucifixes have remained on the walls.
"We thank divine providence that the crucifix has returned to schools, public offices and hospitals," the Pope told the crowd from a wooden altar platform shaped like a typical local chalet.
"May it ever remain there. May it remind us of our Christian dignity and national identity, what we are and where we are going and what our roots are," he said.
The Church enjoyed great prestige before 1989 among Poles, 90 percent of whom are at least nominally Catholic, because of its defence of human rights during communist rule.

But when pro-Catholic parties won power in democratic Poland, their moves to restore property and grant privileges to the Church aroused resentment, which was skilfully used by the ex-communists to help their election victory in 1993.
